tagline: A desert approach to Sedona, with sandstone and creek habitat nearby
intro: SR 89A approaches Sedona through desert on a divided highway, with access to Red Rock State Park before it reaches the city. At the park, a red sandstone canyon holds a stretch of Oak Creek; preserving its streamside habitat is the park’s main mission.

The larger highway took shape in stages. In 1927, its route became state highway SR 79, though only the Prescott-to-Clarkdale portion had been built. The road reached Sedona by 1929, still unpaved; by 1938, pavement covered the entire route. It became US 89A in 1941 and SR 89A in 1993.

Driving toward Sedona from Cottonwood, the highway heads northeast, passes the access to Red Rock State Park, and remains divided until Sedona. In the city it continues east, with access to Sedona Airport before meeting SR 179.

moments.title: Sedona Wetlands Preserve
moments.text: Six artificial basins make water habitat beside Sedona’s wastewater treatment facility. The preserve covers 27 acres, with 12.2 acres of water distributed among its six basins. The preserve was dedicated in September 2013, and its ponds receive treated effluent from the neighboring plant. The basins help that water evaporate and pass through plants by evapotranspiration. Islands were built in some ponds for wildlife to inhabit and breed, while native wetland plants were added to attract animals and prevent erosion. Ducks and shorebirds draw birdwatchers here because those birds are usually absent from the surrounding dry country.

moments.title: Red Rock State Park
moments.text: Oak Creek runs for 1.4 miles through Red Rock State Park, beneath trees including Fremont cottonwood, Arizona sycamore and velvet ash. The land was once part of Smoke Trail Ranch, purchased in 1941 by airline executive Jack Frye as a retreat for himself and his wife Helen. After later ownership changes and a land exchange, the park opened in October 1991. Its central purpose is protecting creekside habitat, with environmental education and limited passive recreation alongside that work. Away from the creek, the dominant trees change to velvet mesquite, netleaf hackberry, Utah juniper and alligator juniper.

moments.title: Sedona
moments.text: Sedona’s sandstone has played places far beyond Arizona. More than sixty Hollywood productions used the area from the early years of filmmaking into the 1970s, passing its surroundings off as Texas, California, Nevada and even the Canada–US border. The pink rock itself is local: the Schnebly Hill Formation is a thick sandstone layer found only in the Sedona vicinity, deposited during the Permian Period. The city’s name honors Sedona Schnebly, whose husband Theodore Carlton Schnebly served as its first postmaster. Sedona began developing as a tourist destination, vacation-home community and retirement center in the 1950s.
